intro: Ten verses in three unequal blocks: a two verse claim about who owns the world, a four verse entrance liturgy asking who may go up, and a four verse dialogue at a gate that is mostly repetition. This is the Sunday psalm, the shir shel yom for the first day of the week, and in Ashkenazi practice it is sung on weekdays while the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark, which is where most people first meet it. Watch how much of it is questions: three verses out of ten ask something, and in each case the answer comes from another voice.

stichs.en: Of David, a psalm.
The earth is the LORD's, and all that fills it,
the world and those who live in it.

verses.summary: The opening move is ownership, stated at full width before anything narrows it. Two pairings, what fills the earth and who lives in the world, leave nothing outside the claim.

stichs.en: For He founded it upon the seas,
and established it upon the rivers.

verses.summary: The reason given for the ownership is the act of founding. Seas and rivers are what the ancient picture placed under the land, so this is a sentence about foundations rather than about geography.

stichs.en: Who may go up the mountain of the LORD,
and who may stand in His holy place?

verses.summary: The question that turns a cosmology into a liturgy. Having said the whole earth belongs to Him, the psalm asks who is admitted to one small hill of it.

stichs.en: One clean of hands and pure of heart,
who has not lifted up his soul to what is empty,
and has not sworn to deceive.

verses.summary: The answer is entirely ethical. Nothing about sacrifice, nothing about lineage: two conditions of character, then two things the candidate has not done with a spoken word.

stichs.en: He will carry away a blessing from the LORD,
and righteousness from the God of his deliverance.

verses.summary: The reward is built on the same verb as the disqualification just before it: what the man did not lift up in verse 4 is what he gets to carry away here.

stichs.en: This is the generation of those who seek Him,
who seek Your face, Jacob. Selah.

verses.summary: A class of people is named, not an individual. The verse ends on a proper noun that many translations quietly convert into a phrase, which is a translation decision worth being able to see.

stichs.en: Lift up your heads, O gates,
and be lifted up, you ancient doorways,
that the King of glory may come in.

verses.summary: The scene changes without warning to a gate that has to make itself taller. The imperative is addressed to architecture, not to the people standing in front of it.

stichs.en: Who is this King of glory?
The LORD, strong and mighty,
the LORD, mighty in battle.

verses.summary: The challenge from the gate and its answer. The titles handed back are military, which is not what four verses about clean hands and honest speech had prepared.

stichs.en: Lift up your heads, O gates,
and lift them up, you ancient doorways,
that the King of glory may come in.

verses.summary: The repetition is not identical. The second imperative is a plain lift where the first was a passive be lifted, so this is a second knock at the same door with the grammar changed.

stichs.en: Who is He, this King of glory?
The LORD of hosts, He is the King of glory. Selah.

verses.summary: The question comes back with one extra word in it, and the answer drops the battle language for the name of hosts. The psalm ends on the title it has been circling since verse 7.

pardes.body: Three blocks. Verses 1 and 2 claim ownership of everything and ground the claim in an act of founding. Verses 3 to 6 are an entrance liturgy: a question at the gate, a list of conditions, a blessing for whoever meets them. Verses 7 to 10 are a second entrance, this time for the King rather than for the worshipper, built as call and response, which is why the same lines return with small changes instead of new material. The conditions of verse 4 repay slow reading, because not one of them is ritual: {{4.1}} is about hands, and the two clauses after it are about what a person does with his word.

{{4.8}} is written as "my soul", meaning God's own self, and read aloud in the synagogue as "his soul"; printed Bibles carry both forms. The written text makes the clause a warning about carrying the divine self in vain, close to the third commandment, while the read text makes it about a man who stakes his own life on something empty. Neither reading has pushed the other out. Note also that the verb of {{4.6}} and the verb of {{5.0}} are the same root: what the man refused to lift is what ends up lifting him. {{7.5}} is usually rendered "everlasting", though the noun names duration rather than antiquity, which is why both ancient doors and eternal doors are defensible.

The Mishnah in Tamid lists this psalm as the one the Levites sang in the Temple on the first day of the week, and the Talmud explains that assignment by the first day of creation, when God acquired the world and ruled it alone. That is why the psalm opens on possession rather than on praise. The gate dialogue of verses 7 to 10 is widely read as accompanying a procession, and the ark entering the city in Second Samuel 6 is the scene usually attached to it, though the psalm names no occasion of its own. In Ashkenazi practice these verses are sung on weekdays as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark, which turns the gates into the doors of that cabinet and the entering King into a scroll being put away.

The gates that have to lift their heads are read as an image of a vessel enlarging itself for what is about to enter, since nothing can be received by a container measured for something smaller. On that reading verses 7 to 10 are two stages rather than one repeated stage: the first opening is requested, the second is performed. The title in {{10.6}}, hosts, names God through multitude, and placing it at the end of a psalm that began with a single owner of everything closes the circle. The one and the many turn out to be the same claim seen from its two ends.
